conditions: TACITO trial (mRCC, FMT from ICI responders)
external_ask: Search for human dietary intervention trials (e.g., high fiber, polyphenol) in solid tumors receiving ICI that report both gut microbiome compositional changes AND clinical efficacy outcomes (response rate, survival) in the same cohort, establishing a direct correlation or causal link within humans.
limits: 需要找到一项人类饮食干预试验，其中不仅报告了微生物组组成的具体变化（如特定菌属/种群的丰度改变），且这些变化与患者自身的ICI临床疗效（如ORR、PFS或OS）有明确的统计关联或因果分析。目前的材料仅提供了免疫表型变化（DIET）或动物模型验证（DIET, BEWELL），未能在同一人类队列中完成“饮食->微生物组->临床疗效”的直接闭环验证。
question: 在人类 ICI 治疗队列中，是否有干预性研究证实特定饮食模式（如高纤维）通过改变微生物组直接改善了 ICI 疗效？
read_focus: 重点检索DIET试验的全文或其他相关出版物，看是否包含人类参与者的16S或宏基因组测序数据及其与疗效的相关性分析；同时确认BEWELL研究中是否有亚组分析涉及临床结局。
still_missing: The success criterion requires reporting microbiome changes alongside ICI efficacy to establish a causal chain (diet -> microbiome -> efficacy). While this study is the specific interventional trial design needed, the supplied text does not report the primary outcome data regarding microbiome structure or function changes, nor does it present mediation analysis linking microbiome shifts to the observed clinical benefits (EFS, ORR). Therefore, based solely on this text, the mechanistic link 'via microbiome changes' remains unconfirmed, even though the interventional efficacy signal is present.
usable_content: This study conducted a proof-of-principle randomized controlled trial with fully controlled feeding in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). It compared a High Fiber Diet Intervention (HFDI, ramped to 50 g/d) against a healthy control diet (20 g/d). The authors reported exploratory cancer-specific outcomes showing that in the combined neoadjuvant/unresectable cohort (n=24), the HFDI arm had a median event-free survival (EFS) not reached versus 20 months in control (p=0.03), and an objective response rate (ORR) of 77% versus 29% (p=0.06). In the adjuvant cohort, recurrence rate was 14% (HFDI) versus 33% (control). Any grade immune-related adverse events (IRAEs) were lower in the HFDI arm (71.4% vs 93.3%). The study design explicitly states the primary objective was to establish effects on gut microbiome structure and function, confirming the trial was designed to test the diet-microbiome-efficacy axis. 这项研究（DIET 试验，NCT04645680）是一项在黑色素瘤患者中进行的二期随机双盲饮食干预试验，比较了高纤维饮食（30-50 克/天）与健康对照饮食（20 克/天）对免疫检查点阻断（ICB）疗效的影响。摘要报告了早期结果显示高纤维饮食干预可行且治疗结果有改善前景。研究通过外周血单核细胞（PBMC）分析发现，高纤维组在第 5-8 周循环单核细胞、树突状细胞减少，效应记忆 T 细胞增加，且 T 细胞激活信号通路增强。此外，研究进行了人至小鼠的粪便微生物移植（FMT）实验，接受高纤维饮食后患者粪便的小鼠表现出更好的 ICB 反应和类似的免疫细胞变化，提示这种益处具有微生物组依赖性。 This study describes a proposed prospective dietary intervention clinical trial design targeting melanoma patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). The authors plan to implement a sequential intervention involving a high-fermented food diet followed by high-fiber supplementation. The study aims to longitudinally assess gut microbial signatures and evaluate distinct immunological, proteomic, and metabolomic effects associated with these dietary modifications. This study conducted a randomized, cross-over dietary intervention trial (BEWELL Study) in humans, administering black raspberry (BRB) nectar versus a matched placebo. The authors reported that the BRB intervention significantly increased the abundance of Lachnospiraceae in the human gut microbiome, with less physically active participants showing a greater increase. To assess the functional impact on immunotherapy, stool samples from participants (pre- and post-intervention) were transferred into tumor-bearing mouse models (mc38, CMT167) which were then treated with anti-PD1. The mice receiving post-BRB human stool exhibited smaller tumor volumes compared to those receiving pre-BRB stool. Additionally, culturing and supplementing a specific Lachnospiraceae isolate into pre-BRB stool recapitulated the improved response to ICB in the mouse model. This establishes a mechanistic chain where a specific human dietary intervention alters the microbiome, and that altered microbiome confers improved ICI efficacy in a preclinical model. The authors plan to implement a sequential intervention involving a high-fermented food diet followed by high-fiber supplementation. The study aims to longitudinally assess gut microbial signatures and evaluate distinct immunological, proteomic, and metabolomic effects associated with these dietary modifications. This study conducted a proof-of-principle randomized trial (NCT04645680) in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), comparing a fully controlled high-fiber diet intervention (HFDI, 30-50 g/d) against a healthy control diet (20 g/d). The authors reported exploratory clinical outcomes showing that in the combined neoadjuvant/unresectable cohort, median event-free survival (EFS) was significantly longer in the HFDI arm versus control (not reached vs 20 months, p = 0.03), and objective response rate (ORR) showed a favorable trend (77% vs 29%, p = 0.06). Any grade immune-related adverse events (IRAEs) were lower in the HFDI arm (71.4% vs 93.3%). This material provides direct evidence that a specific dietary pattern can be implemented via controlled feeding and is associated with improved clinical efficacy and toxicity profiles in an interventional setting. This study conducted the Phase II Diet and Immune Effects Trial (DIET, NCT04645680), a randomized double-blinded dietary intervention in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Patients were randomized (2:1) to a high fiber diet (30-50 g/d) versus a healthy control diet (20 g/d). The authors reported early results showing the intervention is feasible with promising improvements in treatment outcomes. While the primary human data focused on peripheral immune profiling (showing reduced circulating monocytes and increased effector-memory T cells in the high fiber arm), the study included translational human-to-mouse fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) studies. In these FMT experiments, mice receiving stool from patients post-high fiber intervention demonstrated improved ICB response compared to pre-intervention stool, suggesting microbiome-dependent benefits. The authors conclude that the high fiber diet mediates regulation of peripheral immunity during immunotherapy in a microbiome-dependent manner. This study conducted a randomized, cross-over dietary intervention trial (BEWELL Study, NCT04267874) in which participants consumed black raspberry (BRB) nectar versus placebo. The authors reported a significant increase in the abundance of Lachnospiraceae in human stool following the BRB intervention. To assess the impact on immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) efficacy, participant stool samples (pre- and post-intervention) were transferred into tumor-bearing mouse models (MC38, CMT167) treated with anti-PD1. The study found that stool collected after the dietary intervention was associated with smaller tumor volumes in mice compared to pre-intervention stool, and specific Lachnospiraceae isolates supplemented into pre-intervention stool recapitulated this tumor suppression. This provides a human-derived dietary intervention linked to microbiome changes that functionally enhance ICI response in a preclinical model. The authors found that antibiotic exposure was associated with reduced objective response rate (ORR), shorter overall survival (OS), and shorter progression-free survival (PFS). In contrast, probiotic use was associated with improved ORR, OS, and PFS. FMT combined with ICIs achieved a pooled ORR of 0.30. These results quantitatively support the general concept that gut microbiota modulation influences ICI efficacy and survival outcomes in human cohorts.
